source.title: Scale-Dependent Collective Adaptation in Self-Amending LLM Societies: A Cross-Family Study of Emergent Governance
source.authors: Kazuya Horibe; Masaomi Hatakeyama; Gen Masumoto; T. Hashimoto; P. Romero

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares task outcomes across model sizes, bearing on downstream performance predictability, but measures collective governance in Nomic rather than held-out cross-entropy or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. but does not measure pretraining loss, fit scaling laws, test extrapolation of loss, or estimate compute-optimal allocations. Rows below cover its own Nomic adoption and winner-rate results across scales; the many other reported measures concern rule dynamics or internal representations rather than the downstream-performance measure catalogued here.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Kaplan and Hoffmann only as background, saying scaling laws predict monotonic gains on token-level objectives. It measures no loss, fits no scaling law and estimates no compute allocation. Its scale comparison is of collective process measures in homogeneous five-copy self-play Nomic societies: adoption rate, winner-producing trials, vote mix and rule-set change. The authors say they deliberately do not measure 'which model plays best' but rule-dynamics richness. Higher adoption is not better task performance. Winner rate measures game closure in self-play, not one model's success on a task. So these measures are a related but different construct (multi-agent institutional dynamics), not downstream task performance as V6 names it. The finding is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that collective adaptation in self-amending LLM societies is non-monotonic in scale: one family-specific mid-scale sweet spot (Qwen3.5 4B, Gemma3 12B), rule-inert small models, and veto-heavy or narrow large models. Mixed-size societies collapse into gridlock. Regime classes survive temperature and voting-rule perturbations, though endpoints shift. Probe decodability is necessary but not sufficient, and hidden-state divergence does not predict behaviour. They stress that the regularity is the non-monotonic shape, not the optimum's location.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates multi-agent Nomic governance across model sizes; it does not use the original studies’ held-out-loss measurements or scaling-law fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that changing the voting schedule shifts some endpoints, and that temperature changes operating points while preserving the cross-scale ordering.

fits_no_version.finding: In homogeneous five-copy Nomic self-play, adoption and winner rates peak at one mid-scale per family (Qwen3.5 4B: 33.8%, 8/15; Gemma3 12B: 53.9%, 3/15). Smaller models are rule-inert and larger ones veto-heavy or narrow. The pattern holds under a temperature sweep and majority-from-start voting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Collective rule-amendment dynamics in homogeneous LLM societies are non-monotonic in model size within a family (inverse/U-shaped scaling of a multi-agent behaviour).

record.problems: The paper reports 15 trials per primary condition and notes that cross-scale contrasts may be affected by multiple comparisons and homogeneous self-play. The behavioral rows above do not report confidence intervals or other uncertainty estimates. Results concern two model families and one governance task, not language-model pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted other reported outcomes to keep rows focused on adoption and winner rates: change-type mix, active-rule counts, vote rates, scores, trajectory and reversal measures, and mixed-size societies. Also omitted temperature-sweep values, vote-probe results, and hidden-state divergence because they do not directly measure the scale relationship in downstream task performance catalogued here.

untested.parts: All: no extrapolation of fitted laws.
All: no shape variation at fixed parameter count.
All: no other modality or regime fitted.
No downstream task performance measured versus scale or loss; only multi-agent collective process measures.

record.verdict_notes: This is not a test of scaling laws: the scale contrast concerns multi-agent self-play process measures that the authors themselves frame as not performance. The reader's V6 labels are dropped. Caveats the authors note: self-play confound, n=15 per condition, and multiple comparisons. Table G3 lists Qwen3.5 27B under majority-from-start as 'Yes (target lowered)' for regime change, while the text says no scale changes regime. The model families are instruction-tuned checkpoints, so scale is not isolated from post-training.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute; bottleneck conditions; power-law fit.
Prediction of larger-run loss from fits on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocations and their exponents.
Architecture changes at fixed parameter count and their effect on loss.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The study tests Nomic collective-adaptation outcomes across model scales, not a range of conventional downstream benchmarks or performance as a function of pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices or training setup.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Baseline homogeneous societies across the tested Qwen3.5 and Gemma3 scales
reader_labels.reason: Adoption and winner outcomes peak at family-specific mid-scales rather than improving predictably with each scale increase; see B-Q08-A through B-G27-W.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The scale profile remains broadly non-monotonic, but some endpoints change with the voting rule, including reduced Qwen3.5 4B wins, additional Qwen3.5 27B wins from lowering the target, and increased Gemma3 12B wins; see M-Q4-W, M-Q27-W, and M-G12-W.
